newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers reaffirm political resolve on EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers reaffirm political resolve on EMU.

text.p: The political determination to see a single European currency launched in 1999 appears as solid as ever after EU finance ministers this weekend took another step forward in building monetary union.

Coming after a week in which German Chancellor Helmut Kohl announced that he will run for re-election in 1998, the gathering of ministers and central bankers from the 15-nation bloc appeared to receive a much-needed shot in the arm.

Doubts over a timely start to economic and monetary union have festered in recent weeks, fuelled partly by Germany's sluggish economy and apparent fractures among some EU policy-makers over the wisdom of proceeding on schedule.
But at the very highest level, there was no questioning the commitment to keep EMU on track, and the ministers reached agreement on a number of outstanding issues.
"Economic and monetary union is well on course. We are at the finishing gate," European Commission president Jacques Santer told a news conference Saturday.

Most important, the group said the decision on which countries join the single currency would be made in late April or early May 1998. The strong hint by some was that the fateful decision would be made over the long weekend of May 1.
At least six to eight countries are seen forming the single currency in 1999, including Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, and possibly Ireland and Finland.
In addition, the group settled differences on a Stability and Growth Pact, a measure designed to keep a lid on public spending by governments inside monetary union.
Governments which run budget deficits above 3 percent of Gross Domestic Product could face a series of fines totalling as much as 0.5 percent of their Gross Domestic Product.
Lastly, agreement was reached on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism, dubbed ERM 2, linking the single currency, the euro, to those not among the first wave of participants in 1999.
Despite the impressive political resolve shown in this Dutch coastal town Saturday, several important hurdles for EMU are still ahead, notably in Germany, the linchpin to the entire project.
While recent German economic figures have painted a somewhat brighter outlook, important news on the jobs front is due on April 8 with the release of March unemployment data.
The broad expectation is for a slight reduction in the record level of joblessness, the highest seen since the 1930s.
Should the figures disappoint, financial markets are likely to question again whether Bonn can bring its 1997 budget deficit down to three percent of GDP, the Maastricht treaty's target.
May is also likely to be a critical period for Germany because an important estimate of government tax revenues by a commission of experts is due towards the middle of the month.

In a recent report, economists at J.P. Morgan noted that "the event is awaited anxiously, because the government must accept the commission's estimate for tax receipts as the basis for its budget projection."

Drastic downward revisions to revenue projections would undoubtedly force Bonn to consider a package of additional spending cuts -- in an environment where there is already strong public resentment to the sacrifices for EMU.

Political analysts say this tough balancing act -- the need to keep public finances under control while maintaining public support for European integration -- will prove to be Chancellor Kohl's greatest challenge.
